title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Departs U.S. for Spain, Ending Contentious Legal Battle
snippet: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant whose erroneous deportation to a notorious supermax prison sparked a major legal battle, has left the United States for Spain.
content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran native whose wrongful deportation and subsequent detention in a Salvadoran supermax prison became a national lightning rod over U.S. immigration policy, departed the United States for Spain on Tuesday evening.

Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight accompanied by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez, his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and advocates from the advocacy organization We Are CASA, officials confirmed. His departure brings an end to a protracted legal fight involving federal judges, the Department of Homeland Security, and the U.S. Supreme Court.

A Release in Freedom

In a statement issued ahead of his flight, Abrego Garcia expressed relief at the outcome, saying he was leaving the U.S. "happy" and "with his freedom."

"In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible," Abrego Garcia stated.

While the full terms of his departure remain confidential due to a sealed order signed Friday by U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, government officials confirmed he flew out on a commercial airliner. Administration officials characterized the move as a resolution to months of removal proceedings.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin publicly celebrated the departure, referring to it as a self-deportation while repeating previous claims regarding Abrego Garcia's alleged gang ties—allegations his defense team has repeatedly denied. Department of Homeland Security officials added on social media that Abrego Garcia paid for his own travel and remains permanently barred from re-entering the United States.

Months of Controversy and Court Orders

Abrego Garcia's case gained national attention after immigration officials acknowledged his deportation to El Salvador in March 2025 was an administrative "error." An immigration judge had granted him withholding of removal in 2019 due to credible threats of persecution by gangs in his home country. Despite that protection, he was sent to El Salvador's notorious Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).

Following orders from Judge Xinis and a ruling by the Supreme Court requiring the federal government to facilitate his release, Abrego Garcia was brought back to the U.S. in June 2025. Upon his return, the Justice Department unsealed criminal human smuggling charges against him connected to a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. However, a federal judge dismissed those charges in May, ruling the prosecution was vindictive. That decision is currently under appeal by federal prosecutors.

For months, federal authorities sought to deport Abrego Garcia to various third-party nations in Africa, including Liberia, Uganda, and Ghana, while rejecting his request to relocate to Costa Rica. His departure to Spain effectively concludes one of the most high-profile immigration disputes in recent years.
